AI Stocks Resume Their Slide
 
Plus, the Fed weighs AI jobs scenarios and Tyson improves its beef outlook
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
SOEREN STACHE/DPA/ZUMA PRESS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Tech stocks dropped sharply to start the week. With declines for the likes of Microsoft, Alphabet, Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and others, the S&P 500 was off by 1.9% on Monday, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average held up a bit better, shedding 739 points, or 1.4%.

 

Nvidia’s board isn’t considering a reunion. Despite some investors calling for Jensen Huang to quickly return as chief executive following his resignation last week, the Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia’s board is not considering such a reinstatement. Nvidia shares fell a further 4.1%, bringing its market value below $3.8 trillion. Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday.

 

The Federal Reserve is contemplating a range of scenarios for the AI economy. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said the central bank’s jobs task force is looking at different scenarios for how AI could reshape the economy, including considering whether workers will be displaced. Treasury yields fell, with the 10-year yield dropping 0.03 percentage point to 5.122%.

 

Tyson Foods led the S&P 500’s gainers. Shares of the meatpacker jumped almost 9% on Monday. The company said it expects trends in its beef business to improve, benefitting in part from more a more reliable cattle supply outlook.

 

The set-it-and-forget-it trade in AI is over, investors say. After seeing baskets of AI-related stocks surge again and again in recent years, or what Goldman Sachs researchers referred to as “One Big Trade,” recent volatility and divergence are causing even hedge-fund managers to prepare for a new era in markets.

One Big Story

 
 
SUSAN MONTOYA BRYAN/ASSOCIATED PRESS
 

November’s blue wave has thrown a monkey wrench into tech companies’ data-center plans. But some are more exposed than others.

 

Take OpenAI. All of its roughly 14-gigawatt planned data-center capacity is located in states whose governors back a pause in data-center development, according to data compiled by Cleanview. This applies only to projects that haven’t yet begun construction.

 

Given the uncertainty, companies that have spread their bets across many states appear to be better positioned.

 
 
 

What’s Coming Up

 

• Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, the first report since CEO Jensen Huang resigned.

 

• The major economic data report will be U.S. retail sales for October.

 

• St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, New York Fed President John Williams and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack are speaking.

 

• Home Depot and Walt Disney are also reporting earnings.
